slides.label: Spanning Oriented Subspaces
slides.notes: Open the lecture by naming Chapter 2 as the pre-metric foundation. The point is not to replace vectors with notation, but to let lines, planes, and volumes become computable objects with attitude, orientation, and weight. Anchor the assigned span, printed pages 23-64 and PDF pages 55-96, so students know exactly what this deck covers.

slides.label: The Nonmetric Contract
slides.notes: Set the rule of the game before formulas appear. In this chapter, length, angle, perpendicular normal vectors, and orthonormal bases are deliberately withheld. That restriction is productive because it reveals which geometric facts come from spanning alone: dependence, orientation sign, incidence, and relative full-grade measurement inside a common carrier.

slides.label: Attitude Orientation Weight
slides.notes: Use the line element as the smallest example of the vocabulary that will scale to higher grades. Attitude is the carrier line, orientation chooses one of the two senses along that carrier, and weight records relative amount. Stress that the same three words will describe bivectors and trivectors without changing language.

slides.label: Outer Product Builds Area
slides.notes: Introduce the outer product as the operation that turns spanning into an algebraic object. Antisymmetry makes repeated directions vanish, bilinearity makes area scale correctly with either vector, and associativity lets the same construction climb from line elements to oriented area and volume elements.

slides.label: Orientation Lives In Order
slides.notes: This is the first sign discipline students must internalize. Swapping vector factors does not draw a different carrier plane, but it reverses the orientation of the same plane element. The algebraic minus sign is therefore not decoration; it is the encoded difference between two traversal orders.

slides.label: Same Bivector, Many Shapes
slides.notes: Separate the bivector from any favorite parallelogram. A drawn boundary is only a representative used by the screen. Shearing the factors can preserve the same oriented area element in the same carrier, so the algebra remembers attitude, orientation, and weight while forgetting the accidental corner shape.

slides.label: Area Ratios Solve Coordinates
slides.notes: Connect the wedge product to a familiar linear algebra task without letting coordinates take over. If x is decomposed in the basis a and b, wedging with the opposite basis vector kills one coefficient. The remaining ratio compares two same-attitude bivectors, which is why the result is scalar before a metric appears.

slides.label: Line Intersection By Bivectors
slides.notes: Show that the same area-ratio idea is not confined to origin-based examples. Offset planar lines are reconstructed from anchors and directions by comparing oriented parallelograms in one plane. The computation uses differences and bivector ratios, not normal vectors or Euclidean distance to the lines.

slides.label: Direct Subspace Representation
slides.notes: Make the containment test feel like incidence geometry. A candidate vector lies in a blade-represented subspace exactly when adding it by the outer product fails to raise the span. The zero result means the direction was already present, but it must be interpreted in the grade context that produced it.

slides.label: The Grassmann Ladder
slides.notes: Use the grade ladder to organize the new objects. Grade zero is not outside the algebra; it is the scalar layer. Grade one is vectors, grade two is bivectors, grade three is trivectors, and the binomial counts explain why the pseudoscalar is the unique top-grade attitude in a fixed ambient dimension.

slides.label: Blade Or General k-Vector
slides.notes: Pause on the distinction because later models use four and five algebraic dimensions. Every blade is a homogeneous k-vector, but a sum of k-blades may fail to represent one flat k-dimensional subspace. The four-dimensional example e12 plus e34 is valid algebra but not a single plane.

slides.label: Measurement Stays Local
slides.notes: Clarify what measurement the chapter does and does not allow. Two full-grade elements in the same carrier differ by a scalar, so ratios of areas or volumes are meaningful. Comparing different carriers requires a metric that tells how attitudes relate, which is exactly why Chapter 3 comes next.

slides.label: Two Sign Operations
slides.notes: Present reversion and grade involution as simple sign bookkeeping that becomes important later. Reversion reverses vector-factor order, so its sign depends on the number of swaps needed. Grade involution flips odd grades. Both operations extend linearly, which makes them reliable on full multivectors rather than only on pure blades.

slides.label: Programming Lab: Drawing Bivectors
slides.notes: Tie the first lab back to orientation. With v1 fixed and v2 rotating, the bivector coefficient crosses zero at parallel alignment and changes sign after the crossing. The picture is a computational version of antisymmetry, not an illustration pasted onto the algebra after the fact.

slides.label: Programming Lab: Backface Culling
slides.notes: Use the graphics exercise as an immediate payoff. A projected triangle is front-facing or back-facing according to the sign of the 2-D outer product of two edge vectors from the same anchor. This test lives entirely in the projected plane, so no 3-D normal vector is needed.

slides.label: Programming Lab: Singularity Detection
slides.notes: Frame the third lab as oriented volume doing topological work. Normalize field samples on a cube boundary, triangulate the resulting directions on the unit sphere, and sum small trivectors. A wrap around a point singularity produces a score near one, while an empty region cancels almost to zero.

slides.label: What Carries Into Chapter 3
slides.notes: Close by distinguishing spanning from measuring. Chapter 2 gives the outer product, grades, orientation signs, blades, and same-carrier ratios. Chapter 3 adds metric products so different attitudes can be compared by lengths, angles, projections, and duals. That separation is the mental model students should carry forward.
